content.title: About
content.content: Creamed egg is a boiled egg whose yolk is replaced with a smooth cream made from milk, cream, and sugar. The dish originated in the 1950s and quickly became a popular dessert in Soviet canteens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Creamed egg was often served at festive menus for New Year and Victory Day.
The cream was made only with whole milk and sugar, without egg yolks.
Original recipes sweetened the cream with honey and sometimes added vanilla sugar.
The dish got the name “egg‑cream” because of its visual similarity to a boiled egg.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Creamed egg provides protein from the egg white, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The milk‑based cream supplies calcium and vitamin D, supporting bone health.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The dish is calorie‑rich, which can be beneficial during periods of high physical activity.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: People allergic to egg whites may experience reactions up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The creamy layer contains a considerable amount of sugar, which may be unsuitable for diabetics or those watching weight.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Cream adds saturated fats, which should be limited in cardiovascular disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve creamed egg chilled, often garnished with berries or dusted with powdered sugar. It can be eaten as a standalone dessert or used as a filling for cakes and pastries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep creamed egg refrigerated, covered with plastic wrap, and consume within 2–3 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or off‑color.
